chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Lucky Millinder: a conductor with a great ear who couldn't read
summary: Millinder could not read music but learned riffs after hearing a rehearsal and conducted with a baton; Horace wrote him 'Hallelujah'.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Lucky Millender. Now that's a guy that was a real character. When I say character, I mean he was funny. I could tell you some stories on Lucky Millender.
Lucky Millinder had a great band. He always surrounded himself. He didn't know a note as big as this room.

But he had a great ear, and Lucky could direct a band. This is what he was primarily known for. He could have you make an arrangement for him, which I did. I made an arrangement -- I won't forget this, because I have the score right here in the house now, called "Hallelujah." (Singing) That one -- and I had it up to tempo, real fast. And he had a big band. So the way he would conduct things at a rehearsal, if you had an arrangement, he would get him a chair and sit to the side and tell you to, you know, take down your arrangement and everything, and you'd play it two, three times. And he would sit back and listen. Then he'd come up and tell you, "Okay, let me have it now." And he would get his little baton just (unintelligible) and he'd get the guys ready. Then he'd stomp it off, kick it off. And he would learn those riffs, and he would accent, then, with the baton.
